scenario: AITA for expecting family time? | This morning I woke up and saw my husband watching video game streams, his typical pastime. Later he said the streamers he was watching were having cash giveaways that required participation to be entered. He continued to watch while he covertly built the kids' bikes in the garage as I had asked, then left to run a last-minute grocery errand for dinner, then came home and went upstairs to watch more streaming. After wrapping gifts, I did dishes and put dinner in the oven, and asked him to turn it off to spend time with me with/without kids. He said no. That the stream was only for today and it is not okay for me to expect him to stop doing what he finds enjoyable just because I want him to do something I find enjoyable. But if I was okay letting him spend $100 on app purchases for this game (same one he's watching) that he'd shut it off no problem. But last year he spent a little over $2,000 on in-app purchases for this game, and after a lengthy discussion, said he wouldn't buy anymore. So I'm not a huge fan of okaying any more money for it. It's almost 6pm and says he doesn't know when it will end, but that there are 2 more streamers left. I feel like the evening is almost over and I am so disappointed and feel saddened that he would rather watch games than spend time with me. Am I an asshole for being upset and having unrealistic expectations?

Scenario:
AITA for expecting family time? | This morning I woke up and saw my husband watching video game streams, his typical pastime. Later he said the streamers he was watching were having cash giveaways that required participation to be entered. He continued to watch while he covertly built the kids' bikes in the garage as I had asked, then left to run a last-minute grocery errand for dinner, then came home and went upstairs to watch more streaming. After wrapping gifts, I did dishes and put dinner in the oven, and asked him to turn it off to spend time with me with/without kids. He said no. That the stream was only for today and it is not okay for me to expect him to stop doing what he finds enjoyable just because I want him to do something I find enjoyable. But if I was okay letting him spend $100 on app purchases for this game (same one he's watching) that he'd shut it off no problem. But last year he spent a little over $2,000 on in-app purchases for this game, and after a lengthy discussion, said he wouldn't buy anymore. So I'm not a huge fan of okaying any more money for it. It's almost 6pm and says he doesn't know when it will end, but that there are 2 more streamers left. I feel like the evening is almost over and I am so disappointed and feel saddened that he would rather watch games than spend time with me. Am I an asshole for being upset and having unrealistic expectations?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This scenario touches on **boundaries, fairness, and emotional needs in relationships**, and your question isn’t about being an "asshole" (which is a binary label that rarely applies in nuanced situations) but rather about **how to navigate expectations, compromise, and resentment**—all of which are healthy parts of a relationship. Here’s my breakdown: --- ### **Is This a Zero (0) or One (1)?** **Answer: 1 (But with caveats—see below).** You’re *not* the asshole for feeling upset, but the issue isn’t just about your emotions—it’s about **how expectations are communicated, enforced, and balanced** in your marriage. The core tension here isn’t about "right" or "wrong" but about **equity, respect, and emotional labor**. --- ### **Why It’s Not a 0 (You’re Not the Asshole)** 1. **Your Needs Matter** - You’re asking for *shared time* with your husband, which is a basic emotional need in relationships. Feeling disappointed when this isn’t prioritized is valid, especially after you’ve already handled most of the household tasks (cooking, cleaning, gift-wrapping, grocery shopping). **Your time and energy are also valuable.** - His justification ("I’m okay with spending $100 but not $2,000") is a classic example of **moral licensing**—where small indulgences justify larger ones. This is a red flag for imbalance. 2. **The Hypocrisy of His Stance** - He’s arguing that *you* shouldn’t expect him to stop an activity he enjoys, yet he’s okay with spending money on it (even if he claims he won’t). This inconsistency suggests his priorities aren’t aligned with yours, and that’s a relationship issue, not a personal failing on your part. 3. **Family Time ≠ Just "Doing Things Together"** - Family time isn’t just about shared activities—it’s about **presence and emotional connection**. If he’s physically present but mentally absorbed in gaming (even while building bikes or running errands), it’s not the same as being *with* you. You’re not asking for perfection; you’re asking for *attention*. 4. **The $2,000 Spending History** - His past behavior (spending thousands on in-app purchases) shows a pattern of prioritizing gaming over financial responsibility. If he’s now saying he won’t spend more, that’s progress—but it doesn’t erase the fact that his current behavior (watching streams for hours) is a continuation of that habit, just in a different form. --- ### **Why It’s Not a 1 (You’re Not the Villain Either)** 1. **His Perspective Has Merit (But Needs Context)** - He’s right that **you can’t expect him to drop everything just because you want attention**. That’s an unrealistic demand. Relationships require **mutual effort**, not one-sided sacrifices. - His argument that the stream is "just for today" is a weak excuse—if he’s doing this regularly, it’s not a one-time thing. But if this *is* an occasional habit, he should still acknowledge your feelings. 2. **The "Enjoyable" Double Standard** - You’re right to call out the hypocrisy: He’s okay with spending money on the game but not time on it. **Money and time are both resources**, and if he’s willing to spend thousands on one but not hours on the other, that’s a problem. - However, his stance that *you* shouldn’t expect him to stop something he enjoys is also flawed. **Relationships require give-and-take.** If he loves gaming, great—but it shouldn’t come at the cost of neglecting his partner. 3. **The Timing Issue** - It’s 6 PM, and he’s still streaming. If this is a daily or weekly habit, it’s not just about tonight—it’s about **how he structures his time**. If he’s always prioritizing gaming over family, that’s a pattern worth addressing. --- ### **The Real Problem: A Lack of Negotiation** This isn’t about "who’s right"—it’s about **how to create a system where both of you feel heard**. Here’s how to reframe the conversation: #### **1. It’s Not About "Expectations" vs. "Freedom"** - You’re not asking him to *never* game. You’re asking for **shared time**—not as a punishment for his gaming, but as a way to **reconnect**. - Instead of saying, *"You have to stop,"* try: *"I’d love to spend some time with you tonight. Can we agree on a time limit for the stream, and then we can do something together?"* - This turns it from a demand into a **collaborative solution**. #### **2. Address the Underlying Issue: Time vs. Money** - His spending on the game is a symptom of a deeper problem: **He’s treating gaming as a primary hobby without balancing it with other priorities.** - Instead of focusing on the $100/$2,000 argument, ask: *"How do we make sure we’re both getting enough time for things we care about?"* - This shifts the conversation from blame to **teamwork**. #### **3. The Emotional Labor Gap** - You’ve handled most of the household tasks *and* emotional labor (cooking, cleaning, gift-wrapping, grocery shopping). **That’s not fair.** - If he’s not contributing equally to the household, that’s a separate issue. But even if he is, **both partners need time to recharge and connect**. #### **4. The "Family Time" Misconception** - Family time isn’t just about doing things *together*—it’s about **being present for each other**. If he’s mentally checked out while building bikes or running errands, it’s not the same as being *with* you. - You’re not being unreasonable for wanting **quality time**, not just shared chores. --- ### **What You Can Do Next** 1. **Have a Calm Conversation (Not in the Heat of the Moment)** - Wait until you’re both relaxed. Say: *"I felt really disappointed tonight because I was hoping we could spend some time together after all the things I did today. I know you love gaming, but I’d love to find a way to balance that with time for us. Can we talk about how to make that happen?"* 2. **Set Boundaries (Without Guilt-Tripping)** - If gaming is taking over his life, suggest: - *"Can we agree on a time limit for gaming on weeknights?"* - *"What if we schedule one ‘us’ activity a week, even if it’s just watching a show together?"* - If he resists, ask: *"What would make you more willing to do that?"* 3. **Address the Money Issue Separately** - If he’s still spending money on the game, that’s a separate conversation. But tie it to the bigger picture: *"I get that you love the game, but I also know how much you’ve spent on it. How can we make sure we’re not just spending money but also spending time together?"* 4. **Reevaluate Your Own Needs** - If he’s not willing to compromise, ask yourself: - *Is this a one-time thing, or is this a pattern?* - *Am I okay with this imbalance long-term?* - If it’s a recurring issue, you may need to **reassess the relationship’s dynamics**. --- ### **Final Thought: It’s Not About "Right" or "Wrong"** This isn’t a morality question—it’s a **relationship management question**. You’re not the asshole for feeling upset, but you’re also not the villain for expecting basic respect and time. The real issue is that **neither of you has clearly defined how to balance your individual needs with shared priorities**. The goal isn’t to "win" the argument but to **find a way to meet each other halfway**. If he’s unwilling to do that, that’s a problem—not because you’re being unreasonable, but because **a healthy relationship requires mutual effort**. Would you say this resonates with your feelings, or do you see it differently?
